final_proof:
**Setup and conventions.** Let $p$ be prime. For $x \in \mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$ write $x = p^{v}\,a/b$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ not divisible by $p$, and set $\nu_p(x)=v$, $|x|_p = p^{-v}$, $|0|_p=0$. We use the standard facts about this norm on $\mathbb{Q}$:
(i) $|p^k|_p = p^{-k}$ for $k\in\mathbb{N}$; $|\pm 1|_p = 1$; $|m|_p\le 1$ for every $m\in\mathbb{Z}$; $|xy|_p=|x|_p|y|_p$.
(ii) (ultrametric inequality) $|x+y|_p\le\max(|x|_p,|y|_p)$, and consequently, if $|y|_p<|x|_p$ then $|x+y|_p=|x|_p$. (Proof of the consequence: $|x|_p=|(x+y)-y|_p\le\max(|x+y|_p,|y|_p)$; since $|y|_p<|x|_p$ the maximum must be $|x+y|_p$, so $|x|_p\le|x+y|_p\le\max(|x|_p,|y|_p)=|x|_p$.)

$\mathbb{Q}_p$ is the completion of $(\mathbb{Q},|\cdot|_p)$: concretely, the set of Cauchy sequences in $(\mathbb{Q},|\cdot|_p)$ modulo the equivalence $(s_N)\sim(t_N)\iff |s_N-t_N|_p\to 0$, with norm $|[(s_N)]|_p=\lim_N|s_N|_p$. All we use is: every Cauchy sequence $(s_N)$ in $\mathbb{Q}$ determines an element $[(s_N)]\in\mathbb{Q}_p$, and $[(s_N)]=[(t_N)]$ iff $|s_N-t_N|_p\to0$. (Equivalently, for any abstract model of the completion: Cauchy sequences of $\mathbb{Q}$ converge in $\mathbb{Q}_p$, and $|\lim s_N-\lim t_N|_p=\lim|s_N-t_N|_p$ by continuity of the norm; the argument below works verbatim.)

**Step 1: $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is uncountable (Cantor).** Let $f:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be any map and write $f(n)=(f(n)_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$. Define $d=(d_k)$ by $d_k=1-f(k)_k$. For each $n$, $d_n\ne f(n)_n$, so $d\ne f(n)$. Hence no map $\mathbb{N}\to\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is surjective. If $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ were countable, there would be an injection $g:\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\to\mathbb{N}$; since $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\neq\varnothing$, fixing $c\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ and defining $h(n)=g^{-1}(n)$ for $n\in g(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}})$ and $h(n)=c$ otherwise gives a surjection $h:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$, a contradiction. (This also covers the finite case, as a finite set injects into $\mathbb{N}$.)

**Step 2: a map $\Phi:\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\to\mathbb{Q}_p$.** For $e=(e_n)_{n\ge0}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ put
$$s_N(e)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}e_np^n\in\mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}\qquad(N\in\mathbb{N}).$$
For $M>N$ we have $s_M(e)-s_N(e)=\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}e_np^n=p^{N+1}m$ with $m=\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}e_np^{\,n-N-1}\in\mathbb{Z}$, so by (i) $|s_M(e)-s_N(e)|_p=p^{-(N+1)}|m|_p\le p^{-(N+1)}$. Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $N_0$ with $p^{-(N_0+1)}<\varepsilon$; then for $M>N\ge N_0$, $|s_M(e)-s_N(e)|_p\le p^{-(N+1)}\le p^{-(N_0+1)}<\varepsilon$. So $(s_N(e))_N$ is Cauchy, and we set $\Phi(e)=[(s_N(e))_N]\in\mathbb{Q}_p$.

**Step 3: $\Phi$ is injective.** Let $e\ne e'$ in $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ and let $k$ be the least index with $e_k\ne e'_k$; then $e_k-e'_k=\pm1$. For every $N\ge k$, since $e_n=e'_n$ for $n<k$,
$$s_N(e)-s_N(e')=\underbrace{(e_k-e'_k)p^k}_{x}+\underbrace{\sum_{n=k+1}^{N}(e_n-e'_n)p^n}_{y}.$$
By (i), $|x|_p=p^{-k}$. Also $y=p^{k+1}m'$ with $m'=\sum_{n=k+1}^{N}(e_n-e'_n)p^{\,n-k-1}\in\mathbb{Z}$ (an empty sum, $m'=0$, if $N=k$), so $|y|_p\le p^{-(k+1)}<p^{-k}=|x|_p$ (this includes the case $y=0$). By (ii), $|s_N(e)-s_N(e')|_p=p^{-k}$ for all $N\ge k$. Therefore $|s_N(e)-s_N(e')|_p\to p^{-k}\ne0$, so the two Cauchy sequences are not equivalent, i.e. $\Phi(e)\ne\Phi(e')$. (In the abstract-completion formulation: $|\Phi(e)-\Phi(e')|_p=\lim_N|s_N(e)-s_N(e')|_p=p^{-k}\neq0$.)

**Step 4: conclusion.** Suppose $\mathbb{Q}_p$ were countable, i.e. there is an injection $\iota:\mathbb{Q}_p\to\mathbb{N}$. Then $\iota\circ\Phi:\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\to\mathbb{N}$ is an injection (composition of injections), so $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is countable, contradicting Step 1. Hence $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is uncountable. $\blacksquare$

(Remark: in fact $\Phi$ lands in $\mathbb{Z}_p$, so even the $p$-adic integers are uncountable.)
